video_title: Brookfield’s Connor Teskey on the Real Bottleneck in the AI Buildout
transcript: Demand has become the critical input to  growth [music] for every major company in   every major country around the world and there is  a scarcity of it. The growth we're seeing across   critical infrastructure assets [music] and the  overwhelming need for energy around the world   goes so far beyond simply artificial intelligence.  Demand is up here and supply is down here. Even if   demand [music] growth was to slow, even  if it was to plateau, even if it was to   decline [music], there would still be a huge  supply demand imbalance to the providers. It   is perhaps the greatest capital need in in the  history of mankind. It's [music] it's pretty   exciting. Welcome to Goldman Sachs Exchanges  Great Investors. I'm Alison Mass. Today I'm   sitting down with Connor Teskey, CEO Brookfield  Asset Management. [music] Connor joined Brookfield   in 2012 at age 24. 14 years later, he runs the  entire asset management business [music] managing   approximately 1.3 trillion dollars across [music]  infrastructure, renewable power, real estate,   private equity and credit while continuing to  lead its energy group. [music] In this episode,   we discuss Connor's transition to the CEO  seat, [music] Brookfield's AI infrastructure   buildout across the US and Europe and  the firm's strategic expansion in credit. Connor, welcome to Great Investors.  It's so fantastic to have you here.   Thank you for having us. So across all  those asset classes that you play in,   is there one that you're most excited about right  now? I I'm probably a little bit biased. Um I   I have spent the last 10 years as as part of the  energy team and a business that's grown very very   rapidly. I still lead that business today. I  think if there was one theme across Brookfield   that is quite dominant right now, it's energy and  infrastructure. And and um, a lot of the in that   space, uh, a portion of it is undoubtedly being  driven by AI and AI infrastructure is a a huge   theme at Brookfield, but the growth we're seeing  across critical infrastructure assets and the   overwhelming need for energy around the world goes  so far beyond simply artificial intelligence. And   that is one that the capital needs are bigger  than at any point in history. It is perhaps   the greatest capital need in in the history of  mankind. A-and the returns are very attractive and   we see this this theme not enduring for quarters  or years, but through the end of this decade and   beyond. It's it's pretty exciting. Yeah. Must  be really fun for the energy team investors to   have you sitting at the table. It, it, it, yes,  and and and energy's just a fun place to play   right now. You know, in in only four or five  years, electricity is something that everyone   took for granted, and now all of a sudden, it is  the single bi-biggest bottleneck to growth for   the greatest companies around the world and  the largest countries around the world. And   uh, being a provider of that i-is uh, an  exciting place to be. So, let's continue on   the theme of AI, which you brought up. What is  your read on the build-out? I-if there was one   headline or or or narrative that we hear  a lot in the market that i-i-is detached   from what we're seeing in the fundamentals  on the ground, it's that the demand for   uh, AI infrastructure and the demand for  the energy that that supports it is in some   way fragile. You know, we we've seen the market  react quite heavily to certain announcements. Oh,   a potentially more efficient model comes out or a  large hyperscale scaler walks away from one of its   multiple thousands of data center leases and the  whole market reacts. That seems a little divorced   from what we're seeing on the ground. Right now,  uh demand is exceptionally high and supply is only   a small fraction of that demand. Demand is up here  and supply is up down here. And and therefore,   even if demand growth was to slow, even if  it was to plateau, even if it was to decline,   there would still be a huge supply-demand  imbalance to the providers uh of those assets and   and those inputs into that ecosystem. So, um  obviously, a a huge amount of discipline is   required. These are huge projects. It's a large  sum of capital that's going to go into the ground   for multiple decades going forward, but the demand  is absolutely overwhelming and not that imbalance   is not going to be disturbed by small changes. The  other thing that we're seeing on the AI side is   so much talk goes to the big numbers  cuz the numbers are, quite frankly,   staggering. Staggering, thank you. Um That is not  the bottleneck. There is no shortage of capital   and there is no shortage of demand. The bottleneck  is who can actually pull these projects out of   the ground. Who has the capabilities to complete  the land development, secure the grid connection,   uh build the power supply, uh build and operate a  a large-scale gigafactory, provide the redundancy.   That is That is the scarce input. It is  not capital. It is not demand. And we are   increasingly seeing the market flow to not just  simply those that can show up with big dollars,   but those that can show up with both big dollars  and big operating capabilities, as well. All   right. So, you've you've already built significant  AI infrastructure in the US, and now you're taking   that push into Europe. So, what is driving that  expansion? And what do you think travels across   the Atlantic well and what doesn't? So both are  going to see very significant build-outs, but   the the origins of those build-outs and the demand  factors are going to be a little bit different. Um   we we can have a thoughtful debate, but of the  15 greatest technology companies in the world,   the vast majority of them are based here in  the United States. And and those corporates   are driving a ton of corporate demand and a and  an organic build-out of the AI infrastructure   in this country. And that's really being driven by  the large technology companies, the hyperscalers,   and and all of society in the United States is  going to benefit from that. What's interesting   is Europe doesn't have that same concentration  of homegrown um large-scale technology companies   that can provide that corporate demand. That  doesn't mean we're not seeing significant growth,   but it's coming from two different places. One,  the large global technology companies, yes,   most of them are American, but they are global. So  they are of course expanding into Europe as well.   But the other demand driver that we think is under  appreciated is we're actually seeing sovereign   step in in places where that corporate demand is  not going to be the catalyst for the AI build-out.   We're seeing the nation-states What is AI? At  its core, it's a productivity tool. It's designed   to drive efficiency and enable more growth.  We're seeing nation-states step in and say,   "We don't want our population, our country to be  left behind in having access to to those tools   and those productivity gains in the future." So  they will actually backstop the build-out of AI   infrastructure. And we've signed agreements  in France, in Sweden, in Qatar, where the   initial off-taker to support the build-out  of AI infrastructure is not a hyperscaler,   but actually a sovereign. And we call that  sovereign AI. And And we see that demand much   more in places outside of the United States and or  Asia Pac, where where you do have those domestic   global technology leaders. That's an interesting  perspective. Sovereign [snorts] AI. Sovereign AI.   So, the power side of this isn't new territory  for you, as as you've talked about. It's where   you started. You built most of the renewables  business that's been long core to Brookfield. But,   the argument has changed. It used to be a climate  case, and now it sounds like more of a commercial   one. Speed to market, availability, energy  security. So, has the thesis changed in your view,   or has the customer changed? What has changed?  A lot has changed in the last 5 to 10 years.   But, the one thing I would say about  our approach that's been quite helpful,   and this existed long before my time, is our  approach has always been driven by commercial.   We don't take technology bets. We don't ever  accept one basis point of return discount because   of the the decarbonization or energy transition  impact of an investment. We think you can make   very attractive risk-adjusted returns that  also provide those benefits to society.   What has changed is demand has become the critical  input to growth for every major company in every   major country around the world, and there is a  scarcity of it. There is a supply-demand imbalance   that started at the end of the last decade,  the late 2010s. Interestingly, at that point,   it wasn't driven by AI. It It was driven by these  global trends of reindustrialization of elect-and   electrification. That created a supply-demand  imbalance that in and of itself was going to   exist for decades and provide multiple  decades of electricity demand growth.   And then, AI took off and took that supply  demand imbalance and exaggerated it even further.   What we would say that we're seeing  in our business is is two things.   Electrons are a commodity. Um but there is a  lot more sophistication around electrons now. Um   counterparties don't just phone up and say they  want power. They want power that's a certain shape   in a certain location from a certain source for  a certain duration. And being able to evolve   and meet those ever-evolving customer needs is  very, very critical to us. And that's leading to   the development of new technologies. I'll tell you  the fastest growing segment of our energy business   right now is energy storage. Um how do you get  the joys of low-cost renewables, but offset the   the the issues of intermittency? You offset  it with energy storage and batteries, which   is undoubtedly the fastest. That wasn't true 5  years ago. The The other thing that we are seeing   is because electricity has been a become  such a critical bottleneck, the largest   buyers and users of electricity around the  world don't always just go to who can provide   it at the lowest cost. It is very negative for a  hyperscaler if they want to turn on a data center,   but the power supply isn't available yet. So,  rather than having 10,000 small suppliers who   may or may not get a project delivered on time or  on budget, we're increasingly seeing the largest   users of electricity increasingly focus  on a smaller number of scale providers   who have the credibility to work through  problems, deliver on time, deliver on budget,   and really can be a partner to them in providing  what is one of the most critical inputs. And   our business over the last five or 10 years, 10  years ago we essentially sold power to utilities   and governments. Today we sell the most majority  of our power directly to corporates. And and   we work very much with those corporates to meet  their evolving needs and our our relationships   with them go beyond individual contracts to  to global scale framework agreements that just   continue to grow and grow over time. That makes  sense. Certainty and ability to deliver. It it it   it's far more value than picking up a penny  here or a penny there on power price. Yep. So,   everything that you've described gets built with  borrowed money, um, which brings me to credit.   Uh, and in your story there's a mix of organic  and inorganic. Uh, you've built a lot in-house,   uh, but you've also bought a majority stake  in Oaktree, Howard Marks's firm, back in 2019,   and now full ownership, plus stakes in several  other managers. So, how do you decide what   you're going to build versus what you're going to  buy? The build versus buy decision is one that we   we make every time we look to grow at Brookfield.  It is always a build versus buy decision. And   in general, we prefer to build it ourselves if we  think we have the capabilities to do so because   it's often less expensive. Uh, and and two, you  you can build it exactly how you want it. Um, Sam   Pollock, who's built our infrastructure business  over the last 20 years, he's built an incredible   market-leading franchise. It it does not have a  peer. If he wants to launch a new strategy, he's   not going to go buy someone else to do it. He's  very likely going to use some internal resources   to build the strategy from the ground up. However,  from time to time we see capabilities that we   think it would be very difficult to replicate  or it would take us too long to replicate   in order to capture what we think is a very large  and and attractive market opportunity. And that   that was exactly Oaktree for us in 2019. We had a  a very large and market leading equity franchise   on the private investment side, but we did feel  that credit was becoming a a core [snorts] pillar   of private markets going forward. And could we  have built a a market leading credit franchise   over, you know, 10 or 15 years? Absolutely. But  we thought it was worth it to to accelerate that   process and in in in hindsight, we think it  was a a great decision and we we couldn't be   more thrilled with the the the partnership with  Oaktree. So, staying on Oaktree for a second,   how did that deal start? And how did you end up  at the center of it? Um like a lot of things,   some some good fortune. Um I actually started  in the private equity group at Brookfield when I   joined when I joined the firm in in Toronto almost  15 years ago. One of the first things I was asked   to review was actually an investment in another  asset manager that was in need for capital. And   I didn't really know where to start. I'd never  looked at an asset management business before.   And after spinning my wheels for probably a  few days, I had this idea which was, well,   if I can understand Brookfield's business model,  I can probably use that as a base case to try and   understand that this other asset manager's model.  And from that initial review, we began as part of   that process, we simply began to track some of the  other publicly traded alternative asset managers   largely to see how Brookfield could be doing  better and how are we doing versus our peer set.   And at the beginning of 2018, we felt that Oaktree  was not trading appropriately in the market. It   was one of the names we tracked relative to the  incredible quality of that that franchise and what   we thought the long-term earnings potential would  would be. And it's funny, I went to Bruce and I   said, "Well, maybe we can just buy some shares  and make a little bit of money." And Bruce said,   "Fine, but you know, maybe think could we  do something a little bit more strategic   with them." And we took that away into our  little lab and came up with this idea of   privatizing the company, but partnering with  the founders and the existing management.   And that was the transaction we did about 12  months later. Yeah, and the rest is history. Yeah,   it's been great. How would you characterize  your approach to making investment decisions   in general? We have incredible resources around  the world, expertise by asset class, by geography.   I think it is very important to try not to be an  expert at everything. On any individual decision,   there is probably someone at Brookfield who is  more of an expert and more informed than I am.   And I think being a great investor is knowing  where that information is and pulling all   that appropriate information in to make the most  informed decision. That that would be point one.   The the second thing is there are no certainties.  There there absolutely are no certainties.   When you get to a level of confidence where things  are extremely likely and largely in your control,   that's when you pull the trigger  and you invest with conviction.   If you try and remove absolutely every risk and  turn every variable into an absolute certainty,   you will have a perfect track record, but you  will make no investments. And I think it is very   important to pass judgment of we are in control of  enough of the variables here and we have certainty   over enough of the outcomes that we have a return  profile that is downside protected and asymmetric   to the upside. And and that's really our investing  style. And and then the last thing I would say is   it's very important to be able to simplify  things. We invest in extremely large assets   on a on a scale that that few around the  world do. These are large businesses.   It's always important to understand the very small  number of key value drivers and understanding   which ones do you have a strong view on, which  ones are you in control of. I think being able   to simplify large but amazing businesses is very  important to making good investment decisions.   So most of our listeners have heard of Brookfield,  but fewer appreciate the range or the scale.   So give us the rundown. And one thing to flag for  any of our listeners who still file you away as a   Canadian company, you're headquartered in New York  now. So tell us a little bit about that journey.   Sure. So today Brookfield is the leading global  alternative asset manager focused on real assets.   The firm and its predecessors were founded in  1899 and yes, our original origins were Canadian,   but as we've become a scaled global financial  firm, we operate in 50 countries around the   world and we're increasingly concentrated  in the global financial centers with our   headquarters here in New York. So we've seen  a lot of transition in the leadership of the   alternative asset management space over the  last 5 years. You recently stepped into the CEO   seat at the asset management business taking  over from Bruce Flatt who built it and who's   still running Brookfield Corporation. So did you  feel ready and how did that transition happen?   So a lot of credit goes to to not only Bruce but  the the other senior leadership of of Brookfield.   This has been an incredibly methodical  incremental continuous transition.   Yes, we announced a change in titles earlier this  year, but the this transition has been happening   for 3 years and it probably has a number of years  still to run and I remember I think we announced   it on a Wednesday, Monday and Friday of that  week didn't feel a whole lot different. It and   I I think it really comes down to to two  things. One, Brookfield has created a   culture where there's incredible senior mentorship  and they really coach young talent up from an   early age and put people in a position to take on  more responsibility early and and be in a position   to win. Um and I was fortunate to have incredible  mentors and be some of the beneficiary of that.   To your question of of whether or not you can feel  ready, I I always feel that a there's a a certain   healthy level of insecurity is good. It it keeps  you sharp, it keeps you focused, but the fact that   it was such a seamless and incremental transition  uh made it feel very easy. Uh you're a new leader   um at a relatively young age and probably a  decade younger than some of your peers who've   been put into similar positions. Um has that been  an advantage? One of the things that um Bruce and   other members of the the senior leadership do  feel is very important at Brookfield is mixing   excellent experience and tenure and and knowledge  with young energy and um that's something we do   across all of our businesses. Um I'm fortunate  coming into the role to have the most amazing set   of uh senior partners and mentors who have  decades of experience that that we can draw on,   but we love to continuously inject young energy  and young perspective into our leadership in   into our decision-making. We think it's one  important for having fresh perspectives,   but two, it's also important to being relatable  to an extremely large workforce of Brookfield   employees that many of whom are on the younger  side as well. So, what was the most useful thing   that Bruce told you that helped you in your first  6 months in the job? Undoubtedly, the thing having   been fortunate to work with Bruce and the other  senior leaders for a number of years now that   that I find most helpful is just how calm and  balanced they are when markets inevitably change.   Um we like to forecast, we like to to do due  diligence, remove risk, things like that, but   markets are always moving. And one of the things  that at at the very beginning you almost feel   a bit unnerved by it, but that then you become  accustomed to it is just the thoughtful, balanced,   moderate approach to adjusting to the evolving  environment that we all work and live in every   day. When Bruce did tell me for the first time  about the succession the succession plan, um   you know, your mind goes to a lot of places very,  very quickly. And I'm sure he said a lot of things   that day. The one that always sticks out to me,  which really grounded me very quickly, is he said,   "Don't worry whether or not you're the right  person. That was our choice, not yours.   We just want to make sure this is what you want  and you're committed to doing it for for decades   to come." And I remember mind going a lot of  different directions, and the second he said that,   immediately things slowed down and and did  it all became a bit more digestible. Yeah,   that's very thoughtful because to your point  earlier about we're all a little insecure,   it takes your insecurity away because you  didn't make the decision, they did. Yeah, I I   I'll be honest, I I use Bruce's line now. Yeah.  No, no, I I think it's a good one. I may have to   incorporate it myself. Um so, how are involved are  you now in the day-to-day investment decisions?   So, uh I sit on all the investment committees,  so oversee any time around the world that that   Brookfield deploys capital, but I think it's  important to recognize, with the scale of our   operation, um how we deploy capital. And the  way Brookfield operates is we source, execute,   and operate in an incredibly decentralized manner.  For every region around the world that we want to   own or invest in assets, and for every asset class  around the world, we have a dedicated local team.   And those teams are empowered to know everything  about that market, go find no know all the themes,   know the value levers that are coming, position  the business to capture that value, see the risks   that are coming, position the business to mitigate  that risk in a very decentralized manner. But we   actually allocate capital in a quite centralized  group. And it's in that way that we can grow fast   and be local in so many markets around the world,  but we can also consolidate all that knowledge to   use that global perspective to allocate capital to  where we see the the best risk-adjusted returns.   So, myself and a number of the members of  the senior team sit on that centralized   investment committee. I always feel it would be  the wrong approach for me to try to be the expert   in a specific asset class or region where we've  got a dedicated team that does it 24 hours a day,   7 days a week, 365 days a year. I'm rarely  questioning underwriting assumptions.   Um we have experts for that. What we do on that  investment committee is think more high-level,   more strategic in terms of our comments and  our feedback. One of the things your question   triggers a little bit is it seems to us a  little bit silly to bet on a competitive   advantage of simply being smarter than everyone  into perpetuity. Uh you want to create structural   and enduring competitive advantages that allow you  to deploy very attractive risk-adjusted returns   at an incredible scale and consistency  that few can match. That is our brand. So,   we spend a lot of time focusing on enhancing those  strategic competitive and enduring competitive   advantages such that it's not just making the  next good investment, it's putting the firm in   a position to make several good investments  in the the years and decades to come. And   that's things like focusing on changes in global  themes, where is capital flowing, do we have   the right people in the right expertise in the  organization? That's where we spend a lot of time.   So, let's widen out a little bit to the  industry. Um what kind of growth do you   expect in alternatives from here? The growth  in the alternatives industry um is going to be   very significant. I I actually think it's very  tough to see a scenario where the allocations   in either the individual market or the  institutional market slow. And very simply, the   the alternatives industry has grown over  the last 20 plus years essentially on um   institutions beginning to and then increasing  their allocation to alternatives. And that's   grown the industry for the last 20 years and that  in and of itself, growing institutional demand   could drive the growth of the industry for the  next decade and beyond. But now there is this   second additional growth lever, which we call  the individual market. That's your your high net   worth or private wealth investor, that's your life  insurance policy or annuity holder, that is your   401k, your your retiring market. In that segment  of the market the the penetration is very low.   If institutional investors are allocated somewhere  in the call it mid-teens range to alternatives and   probably going up to to 20 or 30%over time. Uh  that individual market is 2%or less today. So,   um in terms of directional trend line, we we don't  see it slowing down. And it's it's not a trend   or a fad. It's because of what alternatives can  provide to those investors'portfolios that that   traditional um portfolios don't have. Um private  market investments over the long term do come   with a return premium because they are private  and and there is uh a slight liquidity premium.   But more importantly, they provide a huge amount  of stability uh in portfolios, especially relative   to public markets that are becoming increasingly  volatile. Um secondly, with many uh of the leading   companies around the world staying private longer,  and with certain industries much more concentrated   in the private markets, it can provide diversity  to what they can get in a a public portfolio.   And then at the last thing I would say is private  capital very simply works better for certain   types of investments. Think large infrastructure  projects that are going to take two, three, four,   five years to build and are going to be non-income  producing for that period of time, then they turn   on and they produce cash for the next four or  five decades. It's really different after they're   they're producing cash, and that works really  well in a quarterly over quarter reporting cycle.   Those early years of putting dollars, non-income  producing dollars in the ground, doesn't work   great in the public market. So, whether it's  returns, whether it's stability, whether it's   diversification or access to some of the biggest  growth trends and growth themes around the world,   we view it as directionally a a a pretty strong  certainty that the growth will continue to be   there going forward. Will it ebb and flow over  that very strong growth trend line? Absolutely,   and that that will be driven by markets, that  will be driven by performance of of certain   vehicles and and things like that, but I think  the trend line is is pretty definitive. Yeah.   And as you say, as long as the asset classes  continue to outperform the public market indices   over any periods of time you look at, 1 3 5 10  years, um investments will flow in. Absolutely.   And they've proven to do that over decades. So,  last one before we go to our lightning round.   You were a rower in college, I understand.  So, what did that teach you about leading? Um   feels a long time ago. Uh I I wasted all my time  growing up watching, following, playing sports.   That's not a waste of time. I still spend a lot of  time on ESPN. Um rowing's a kind of a funny sport.   Um there's very little that's actually enjoyable  about rowing itself. It very you get up early in   the morning, you go somewhere that's often cold  or wet in the dark, and you twist your back and   pull as hard as you can 3,000 times in a row. Um  but it is one of the greatest team environments   I think you can get in sports because it really  is an environment where a crew is only as good   as the weakest link, and it doesn't matter if  you're the strongest person in the boat or the   weakest person in the boat. If you do a little  bit better, the whole boat goes faster. And   I think what it teaches you about discipline,  what it teaches you about working really hard,   and what it teaches you about teamwork, I'd say  that those are some of the things we use every day   in a much more different environment that we work  in now. Okay. We like to end these conversations   with sort of a quick answer round. So, what  is your greatest strength as an investor?   Ability to simplify things. And what is the  best advice you've ever gotten from outside the   business? To always remember that this is a people  business. People will always do more deals and   do more business that people they enjoy working  with. This will always be a people business. Yeah,   I agree. People want to do business with people  they like. Yes. And people they trust. Yes.   How do you spend your time out of the office?  And I'm assuming it's not on a boat. No,   no, with my family. I have a very young  family, so 100%of my time out of the office   is with my wife and kids. That sounds fun.  Which investor do you admire most? Sam Pollock.   Built our infrastructure business. Okay. And what  are you most excited about in the world right now?   I wear two hats at Brookfield, um, the asset  management business and the energy business.   It's very fun waking up in industries and  markets where the question is not can you grow?   It's how much can you grow and can you do the  right growth? That is exciting. That That makes   it easy to get out of bed in the morning.  Well, Connor, thank you so much for joining.   Uh, it was a fun discussion and I hope you enjoyed  it as well. Thank you for having us. [music] Thank you all for listening to this episode of  Goldman Sachs Exchanges [music] Great Investors,   which was recorded on Wednesday,  September 16th, 2026. I'm Alison Mass.   If you enjoyed the show, we hope you'll  follow us on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube,   or wherever you listen to your podcasts and  leave us a rating and a comment [music].
